title: Senate Advances Russia-Iran Sanctions Bill With 100% Tariff Threat, China Vows Retaliation Over Robot Ban
subhead: The Senate passed a second procedural vote 84-12 on the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which would authorize tariffs up to 500% on Russia and 100% on countries buying Russian energy. China promised 'resolute retaliation' if the US presses ahead with its FCC ban on Chinese humanoid robots. Meanwhile, the Fed left rates unchanged with three hawkish dissents, and Iran rejected Oman's joint-management proposal for the Strait of Hormuz.

sections.heading: Senate Advances Sweeping Russia-Iran Sanctions Bill
sections.body: The US Senate voted 84-12 on Wednesday to advance debate on the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, clearing its second procedural hurdle after an 86-12 vote on Tuesday. The bill, renamed after the late senator who championed it, would authorize tariffs of up to 500% on Russian imports and up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas — a provision squarely aimed at China and India, two of Russia's biggest energy customers. It also reinserts sanctions on Iran's weapons and energy sectors. Senator Jeanne Shaheen acknowledged Democratic concerns about giving Trump more tariff powers, but argued the bill 'explicitly directs these tariffs for one unambiguous purpose: to increase the pressure on Vladimir Putin.' The Senate aims to complete work on the package by the end of this week, though it will then sit until the House returns from its August recess. Trump voiced support for the bill but said he sees no need for the House to interrupt its recess to consider it promptly, according to TASS.
sections.whyItMatters: If enacted, 100% tariffs on Russian energy buyers would force a structural choice on India and China: continue discounted Russian crude or preserve access to the US market. The bill represents one of the most consequential secondary sanctions mechanisms in decades.

sections.heading: China Vows Retaliation Over US Robot Ban
sections.body: China's commerce ministry said Thursday it will 'resolutely retaliate' if the US follows through on the Federal Communications Commission's ban on new imports of foreign-made humanoid robots and power inverters, which predominantly targets Chinese manufacturers. The ban, announced July 28, covers new models of humanoid and quadruped robots weighing over 4.4 pounds with network connectivity and onboard AI — effectively capturing most of China's roughly 85% share of the global humanoid robot market. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said the move was to 'secure America's critical supply chains.' China's ministry called for the ban's withdrawal, saying it 'severely damages' bilateral relations and constitutes protectionism. The dispute comes weeks before a planned visit by Xi Jinping to meet Trump in September, and compounds existing tensions over chip export controls and AI model restrictions.
sections.whyItMatters: The ban extends US-China tech containment from semiconductors into physical AI hardware — a new frontier. If China retaliates with export controls on rare earths or robotics components, supply chains for US automation and defense could face meaningful disruption.

sections.heading: Fed Holds Rates Steady as Three Dissent for a Hike
sections.body: The Federal Reserve left its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.50%-3.75% on Wednesday, the fifth consecutive hold, but the decision drew three dissents from regional bank presidents (Cleveland, Dallas, and Minneapolis) who favored a quarter-point increase. Chair Kevin Warsh pledged the Fed 'will not waver' on inflation but declined to signal whether a hike is coming, saying only that 'if inflation continues to be elevated through the forecast period, interest rates could well be part of that solution.' Bond markets sent a sharp signal: the 30-year yield crossed above 5.20% for the first time since mid-2007, while the yield curve steepened as 2-year yields fell and long-end yields rose — a signal that markets question the Fed's inflation credibility. Bank of America economists titled their note 'Doved and Confused,' arguing the need to re-establish credibility 'increases the probability that the Fed will hike in September.' CME FedWatch shows a 57% probability of a September hike, down from near-100% priced before the meeting. J.P. Morgan's Michael Feroli called Warsh's remarks 'well-turned phrases but little in the way of a coherent macro view.'
sections.whyItMatters: Three dissents is the most at an FOMC meeting in years, exposing a deepening split on the committee. The simultaneous rise in long-end yields and decline in short-end yields suggests markets are pricing credibility risk, not just rate risk — a more dangerous dynamic for the Fed.

sections.heading: Iran Rejects Oman's Hormuz Proposal, Counters With Its Own
sections.body: Iran has rejected Oman's proposal for joint 50-50 management of the Strait of Hormuz, with Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi telling state TV that Muscat's plan 'did not sufficiently address Tehran's concerns about control of the strait.' Iran's counterproposal would give Tehran management of both inbound and outbound traffic lanes, with Oman managing only part of one route — effectively giving Iran oversight of all commercial transit. Gharibabadi warned the strait 'will remain closed' if Oman rejects the plan. He also insisted that Hormuz could not return to pre-war arrangements where ships transited without any fees. Oman's original proposal modeled voluntary fees on the Strait of Malacca arrangement, which raises about $70 million annually. Iran has reportedly proposed a $1 million per ship 'service fee' — a figure that would be orders of magnitude higher. Meanwhile, Al Jazeera reports Oman is now considering a three-route proposal: one through Iranian waters, one international lane, and one through Omani waters. The American Petroleum Institute has come out firmly against any Hormuz tolls or transit fees.
sections.whyItMatters: The gulf between Oman's $70M Malacca model and Iran's $1M-per-ship fee reveals this is not a logistics negotiation — it is a sovereignty and leverage dispute. Until there is a workable transit arrangement, the Hormuz premium on global oil and LNG shipping will persist.

sections.heading: US Sanctions Iran's Maritime Insurers and Shadow Fleet Tankers
sections.body: The US Treasury Department on Wednesday imposed a new round of Iran-related sanctions targeting the Persian Gulf Marine Insurance Company and the HormuzSafe Marine Services Authority, which Washington described as fronts for Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps. The action also sanctions eight tankers and 10 entities connected to what the State Department called an 'extortion scheme' — forcing commercial vessels to purchase mandatory maritime 'insurance' before transiting Hormuz, with the IRGC creating the very risks the insurance claims to cover. The Treasury also flagged crypto payment evasion as a growing concern in Iran's sanctions-busting operations. The sanctions came on the same day the US resumed military strikes in the region, with US-Saudi forces hitting Iran-backed militia targets in Iraq — the first time Saudi Arabia has publicly joined US air strikes.
sections.whyItMatters: Sanctioning Iran's maritime insurance apparatus targets the financial infrastructure of Hormuz transit control directly. The crypto-evasion angle signals Washington is tracking Tehran's digital-asset workarounds — a growing feature of sanctions enforcement.

sections.heading: IMF Reaches $1.9 Billion Staff-Level Agreement With Bolivia
sections.body: The International Monetary Fund announced a staff-level agreement on a $1.9 billion, three-year financing program with Bolivia, the country's worst economic crisis in four decades. IMF official Joana Pereira said the program is expected to catalyze an additional $3 billion+ from the World Bank, Inter-American Development Bank, and other partners, for a total package exceeding $5 billion. Bolivia's currency has depreciated more than 60% against the dollar since the government lifted a 15-year peg last month. President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of emergency on June 20 after opposition road blockades strangled food, medicine, and fuel supplies. The IMF program focuses on restoring fiscal sustainability, modernizing the exchange rate regime, strengthening social safety nets, and building financial-sector resilience. Bolivia's dollar reserves have been severely depleted by a decade-long collapse in gas production.
sections.whyItMatters: Bolivia's 60% currency crash and depleted reserves made it the most pressing sovereign debt crisis in Latin America. The IMF deal — if approved by the board — provides a framework, but the political resistance from Morales-aligned unions and the scale of the fiscal hole mean implementation risk remains extreme.

sections.heading: Oil Slips Below $90 as Tankers Keep Moving Through Conflict Zones
sections.body: Brent crude fell $1.29 to $89.45/barrel on Thursday, reversing part of a sharp 7.9% rally the previous session, as tanker traffic continued through Middle East conflict routes. 39 commodity ships passed through the Bab el-Mandeb strait into the Red Sea on Tuesday, the highest count since July 19, according to preliminary shipping data. Only a few transited through the Strait of Hormuz. IG analyst Tony Sycamore noted that 'while overall volumes are reduced, oil continues to leak out of the region through multiple channels' and that workarounds are eroding Iran's leverage over Hormuz. WTI fell 56 cents to $83.90. The previous session's spike came after a pause in US-Iran hostilities proved short-lived, with Iran firing on US bases in Jordan and striking three tankers transiting Hormuz on what it called unauthorized routes.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is pricing a persistent but not catastrophic supply disruption. The divergence between Hormuz (barely operational) and Bab el-Mandeb (recovering to near-normal traffic) suggests the Red Sea route is adapting faster than the Gulf, compressing Iran's shipping leverage even as the physical conflict continues.

bottomLine: Three distinct financial fronts moved simultaneously on Thursday. In Washington, the Senate's 84-12 vote on the Graham sanctions bill brings 100% tariffs on Russian oil buyers within legislative striking distance — a structural choice for India and China if it becomes law. In Beijing, the commerce ministry's promise of 'resolute retaliation' over the FCC's robot ban extends the US-China technology conflict into physical AI hardware. And at the Fed, three dissenting votes and a 5.20%+ 30-year yield exposed a committee that cannot agree on whether to hold or hike — leaving markets to price credibility risk instead. Meanwhile, Iran's rejection of Oman's Hormuz proposal means the strait remains in a diplomatic stalemate, even as tankers find workarounds that are slowly eroding Tehran's shipping leverage.
sources: Reuters, Al Jazeera, TASS, Fox News, AP News, Ars Technica, CNBC, Business Standard, Courthouse News, Zawya, Tribune India, WION, CME Group FedWatch, EconoTimes, China Daily
